questions.article: Know Your Rights and Perform Your Duties
questions.q: What “two-point formula” for a successful life does the editorial offer?
options: Avoid both material and spiritual effort
Not quite. The article says: Be content in material things and idealistic in spiritual matters.
Be content in material things and idealistic in spiritual matters
Yes. This gives peace of mind and ends the habit of complaint.
Demand your rights first and do your duties later
Not quite. The article says: Be content in material things and idealistic in spiritual matters.
Be ambitious in wealth and modest in worship
Not quite. The article says: Be content in material things and idealistic in spiritual matters.
questions.rationale: “As regards material things, remain contented, and in spiritual matters, be idealistic.”

questions.q: What does the article call the first principle for understanding Islam?
options: To compare it with other religions first
Not quite. The article says: To distinguish Islam from Muslims – judging Islam by its text, and Muslims by its teachings, not the reverse.
To study the history of Muslim empires
Not quite. The article says: To distinguish Islam from Muslims – judging Islam by its text, and Muslims by its teachings, not the reverse.
To learn from whichever group is largest
Not quite. The article says: To distinguish Islam from Muslims – judging Islam by its text, and Muslims by its teachings, not the reverse.
To distinguish Islam from Muslims – judging Islam by its text, and Muslims by its teachings, not the reverse
Right. The community is not the reference point.
questions.rationale: “You have to judge Islam based on its original text. And, you have to judge Muslims in the light of Islamic teachings and not vice versa.”

questions.q: The article likens nation-building to planting an orchard. What is the point of the comparison?
options: A nation grows best when left alone
Not quite. The article says: A nation grows only through long, patient nurturing of individuals, one by one – not through meetings and slogans.
A nation should export fruit
Not quite. The article says: A nation grows only through long, patient nurturing of individuals, one by one – not through meetings and slogans.
A nation grows only through long, patient nurturing of individuals, one by one – not through meetings and slogans
Well read. “Build the individual and you build the nation.”
A nation needs good soil and rain
Not quite. The article says: A nation grows only through long, patient nurturing of individuals, one by one – not through meetings and slogans.
questions.rationale: “The work of planting an orchard begins by obtaining seedlings and providing every single one with such favourable conditions as will enable it to develop its potential.”

questions.q: A man asked the Prophet for one piece of advice by which to manage all the affairs of his life. What was it?
options: “Do not speak in gatherings”
Not quite. The article says: “Do not be angry”.
“Do not be angry”
Yes. Respond positively even when provoked.
“Do not travel alone”
Not quite. The article says: “Do not be angry”.
“Do not borrow money”
Not quite. The article says: “Do not be angry”.
questions.rationale: “The Prophet replied, ‘Do not be angry.’ It means, don’t get angry even when provoked.”

questions.q: The article compares silence in a moment of anger to “shift time” when driving. What does silence do?
options: It hides the anger from others
Not quite. The article says: Like changing gear, it turns the mind from a rash reaction towards a considered, positive response.
It makes the other person feel guilty
Not quite. The article says: Like changing gear, it turns the mind from a rash reaction towards a considered, positive response.
Like changing gear, it turns the mind from a rash reaction towards a considered, positive response
Well reasoned. “When you are angry, keep silence.”
It brings the matter to an end
Not quite. The article says: Like changing gear, it turns the mind from a rash reaction towards a considered, positive response.
questions.rationale: “At the time of anger, keeping silence is like changing gears of the mind… the result will be a well thought out action instead of a rash harmful reaction.”

questions.q: The Quran calls the peace treaty of Hudaybiyyah a “clear victory.” Why, according to the article, is peace the greater success?
options: Peace opens the door to every kind of opportunity, while political victory gives only control of a territory
Correct. After the treaty the message spread rapidly.
Peace pleases one’s opponents
Not quite. The article says: Peace opens the door to every kind of opportunity, while political victory gives only control of a territory.
Peace costs less than victory
Not quite. The article says: Peace opens the door to every kind of opportunity, while political victory gives only control of a territory.
Peace is easier to achieve
Not quite. The article says: Peace opens the door to every kind of opportunity, while political victory gives only control of a territory.
questions.rationale: “Political victory gives you only one thing and that is administrative control over a piece of land. But peace has much greater potential. Peace opens the door to multiple opportunities.”

questions.q: Why does the article compare decisions in life to catching a train?
options: The destination matters more than the journey
Not quite. The article says: The train leaves on time whether we are ready or not – so one must prepare and decide in time.
The train leaves on time whether we are ready or not – so one must prepare and decide in time
Right. Wavering means being left on the platform.
One should always travel with others
Not quite. The article says: The train leaves on time whether we are ready or not – so one must prepare and decide in time.
Trains are often late, so there is no hurry
Not quite. The article says: The train leaves on time whether we are ready or not – so one must prepare and decide in time.
questions.rationale: “The train is no respecter of persons. It arrives on time and departs on time… we will miss the train of life and be left standing if we fail to get on board by taking timely and right decisions.”

questions.q: In group work, people tend to leave the burden to others. What does the article say produces full commitment?
options: Strict supervision
Not quite. The article says: Seeing the common good as one’s own good.
Seeing the common good as one’s own good
Yes. A deep sense of social consciousness.
Working with friends only
Not quite. The article says: Seeing the common good as one’s own good.
A larger personal reward
Not quite. The article says: Seeing the common good as one’s own good.
questions.rationale: “Only when one has come to think of the common good as one’s own good, of the profit of society as one’s own profit, will one become fully committed to collective work.”

questions.q: A small child is pure by nature. How does the purity asked of an adult differ?
options: It is given by one’s family
Not quite. The article says: It must be regained consciously, by his own effort, after the conditioning of his surroundings.
It is the same, and needs no effort
Not quite. The article says: It must be regained consciously, by his own effort, after the conditioning of his surroundings.
It must be regained consciously, by his own effort, after the conditioning of his surroundings
Well read. Self-attained purity is what is valued.
It cannot be regained
Not quite. The article says: It must be regained consciously, by his own effort, after the conditioning of his surroundings.
questions.rationale: “Now, he must make himself clean and pure spiritually by his own striving… It is this self-attained spiritual progress which is desirable in Islam.”

questions.q: Tiny organisms can do more harm than large, obvious dangers. What does the article compare to them in our lives?
options: Small, repeated moments of negligence that quietly waste time and money and corrode character
Exactly. Trivial for a day; enormous over a lifetime.
Rare but serious accidents
Not quite. The article says: Small, repeated moments of negligence that quietly waste time and money and corrode character.
Unexpected visitors
Not quite. The article says: Small, repeated moments of negligence that quietly waste time and money and corrode character.
Unkind remarks by strangers
Not quite. The article says: Small, repeated moments of negligence that quietly waste time and money and corrode character.
questions.rationale: “Easy going negligence can creep into our souls, like bacteria into the body, and if not pulled up short, can become an ingrained attitude.”
